strengths: MP-Bench addresses a useful multimodal learning problem: connecting atmospheric grids to geographically grounded warning descriptions. Its 421,363 records cover seven severe-weather categories plus normal conditions across 2,412 stations, providing a potentially valuable resource for meteorological pattern recognition.

Preserving hourly information and 37 pressure levels avoids the substantial information loss of daily averages or three-channel visualizations. The temporal gating, geographic masking, and text-conditioned channel weighting provide a coherent adaptation of pretrained multimodal models to these inputs.

Table 3 includes all eight combinations of the proposed modules. The complete configuration improves MC-main accuracy from 42.73 to 57.23, RSW accuracy from 41.25 to 58.63, and NSW score from 1.1 to 1.7, providing evidence that the combined design helps on the evaluated task.

The 2023 training/2024 testing separation is preferable to a random record split. Evaluating four model backbones, reporting category-specific performance, and supplying prompts and training hyperparameters are additional strengths.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not established by the experimental protocol. The Data Alignment section explicitly supplies ERA5 reanalysis from [t, t+11], where t is warning issuance time. These future realized atmospheric fields are unavailable when issuing a warning. The experiments therefore demonstrate retrospective warning reconstruction conditional on subsequent weather, rather than prospective forecasting. Interpreting NWP forecasts could be a valuable application, but no evaluation with forecasts available at issuance time establishes that capability. This mismatch is a principal reason for the weak-reject recommendation.

The main comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution sufficiently. All open-source models in Table 2 already include the three modules, while GPT-4o receives different variables through a three-channel representation and lacks the reported task-specific fine-tuning. Its exceptionally low 0.19/100 T/F accuracy also needs investigation of response parsing and evaluation behavior. Table 3 supplies a useful unmodified baseline, but only under an ambiguously described 5,000-instance sampling protocol. Comparable full-scale baselines using simple grid classifiers, standard spatiotemporal encoders, or text-only inputs are missing.

Aggregate accuracy gives incomplete evidence of useful severe-weather detection. Approximately 88% of records contain warnings; if this proportion carries into T/F evaluation, an always-positive predictor would achieve about 88%, compared with the best reported 87.13%. The actual T/F test distribution is not provided, so this comparison cannot be resolved. Snowstorm accuracy is reported below 6%, and the best nationwide generation score is only 2.1/5. Class-balanced metrics, per-hazard precision/recall, and false-alarm and missed-event rates are needed to substantiate broad effectiveness.

Important dataset construction choices remain unclear. Issued warnings are forecasts rather than verified event outcomes, and the manuscript does not establish that sampled normal records represent confirmed absence of severe weather. It also does not explain how overlapping warnings, multiple hazards in one region, warning validity periods, and national summaries are reconciled with single-answer targets and a fixed 12-hour window. The exact 2024 test subset and its task composition are unspecified.

Reproduction of the core input pipeline remains difficult despite the supplied training settings. The main text lists temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure, whereas the appendix specifies geopotential, u/v wind, temperature, and specific humidity. Normalization, grid dimensions, Gaussian bandwidth, convolution/projection dimensions, and the interface to each pretrained visual encoder are insufficiently specified. The DTGF norm reduction axes and TGS indexing are also unclear. These details materially determine how the proposed architecture operates.

The architectural originality and interpretation claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The modules combine familiar gating, Gaussian masking, and attention operations; their practical combination has value, but attention-weight plots do not establish physical causality or verify atmospheric mechanisms. Several correctable reporting issues further reduce clarity: 36.01 is described as an MC-sub gain although it is the final score, NSW 2.1/5 is called 2.1%, and the judging prompt includes fog while omitting hail. The nationwide metric also lacks validation against human judgments or deterministic matching of its structured outputs.

strengths: MP-Bench is a potentially useful resource for meteorological multimodal learning: 421,363 paired records spanning 2,412 stations, seven warning categories, and normal conditions. Preserving hourly fields and vertical atmospheric structure offers richer inputs than daily averages or surface-only images.

Training on 2023 and testing on 2024 provides a meaningful temporal separation. Experiments across four model backbones demonstrate that the proposed adaptation is feasible beyond a single architecture.

The complete module ablation in Table 3 provides evidence of benefit within the benchmark. Adding all three modules improves MC-main from 42.73 to 57.23, MC-sub from 28.01 to 36.01, and RSW from 41.25 to 58.63. The appendix supplies prompts, dataset statistics, and substantial training configuration information.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not supported by the experimental setup. Inputs are ERA5 reanalysis fields covering [t, t+11] after warning issuance at time t. These retrospectively reconstructed future conditions are unavailable when issuing a warning. The experiments therefore demonstrate retrospective warning-label inference, not prospective severe-weather forecasting. Although the introduction proposes ingesting NWP forecasts, no experiment evaluates that setting or its forecast errors. This is the principal concern determining my recommendation.

Warning issuance is used as ground truth without verification against observed weather. Issued warnings can differ from realized events, and 'no warnings issued' does not establish normal conditions. The manuscript also does not adequately explain how simultaneous warning categories, repeated updates, cancellations, or varying warning validity periods are handled. Consequently, the claimed precise alignment and single-answer classification targets have unresolved validity issues.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. Table 2 compares four adapted, fine-tuned models against GPT-4o receiving a different, reduced meteorological representation. This confounds training, input information, and architecture. The ablation is useful, but its 5,000-instance sampling protocol and relationship to training and testing are unclear, and the input adapter used when all modules are removed is unspecified. Matched conventional meteorological classifiers and text/location-only controls are absent, leaving the necessity of an MLLM and the extent of meteorological grounding uncertain.

The metrics provide limited evidence of useful warning performance under the pronounced class imbalance. Snowstorm accuracy is reported as at most 6%, while gale dominates the dataset. No precision/recall or false-alarm analysis establishes performance on rare hazards. Normal records constitute approximately 12% of the overall dataset, making an always-positive T/F baseline essential; task-specific test distributions are not reported, so the 87.13% T/F accuracy cannot be interpreted confidently. The best nationwide score is only 2.1/5, indicating substantial limitations in the most comprehensive warning task.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. The main text lists temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure, whereas the appendix specifies geopotential, two wind components, temperature, and specific humidity. Normalization across these heterogeneous variables, spatial resolution/cropping, Gaussian bandwidth, and the exact conversion of 185-channel temporal fields into each backbone's input are insufficiently specified. Figure 2 includes a vision encoder whose relationship to the textual architecture description is unclear. These gaps materially limit reproducibility.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Learned temporal and channel weights do not independently establish physical causation or confirm atmospheric variability, and a prescribed Gaussian mask's visualization does not validate learned localization. Evaluation also needs clarification: GPT-4o's reported T/F accuracy is an unexplained 0.19/100; the nationwide judging prompt substitutes fog for hail; and the text describes MC evaluation as four-option selection despite the much larger option list in the appendix. These inconsistencies weaken confidence in the reported scores.

strengths: MP-Bench is a potentially useful resource for meteorological multimodal learning: 421,363 examples cover seven warning categories plus normal conditions, with records from 2,412 stations. Preserving hourly fields and 37 pressure levels offers richer inputs than daily summaries or selected surface-variable images.
The task design spans regional classification, severity identification, and national warning generation. Training on 2023 and testing on a subset of 2024 provides a meaningful temporal separation.

The complete module ablation in Table 3 supports the usefulness of the combined architecture. Relative to the unmodified configuration, MC-main improves from 42.73 to 57.23, MC-sub from 28.01 to 36.01, and RSW from 41.25 to 58.63. Experiments with four language-model backbones also demonstrate implementation flexibility.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not established by the evaluation. Each warning issued at time t is paired with ERA5 reanalysis from [t, t+11], which contains future atmospheric information unavailable at issuance. This supports retrospective interpretation of weather fields, but does not demonstrate early warning from available observations or operational NWP forecasts. The proposed NWP-to-warning application is plausible, yet its forecast-input distribution and errors are never evaluated.

The main comparisons do not adequately establish the method's advantage. Every open-source model in Table 2 includes the proposed modules, while GPT-4o receives a different, reduced input representation without comparable task-specific training. Its reported 0.19% binary accuracy especially requires an explanation of prompting and answer parsing. Table 3 provides valuable controlled evidence, but the role and split of its 5,000 sampled instances are unclear. Matched conventional classifiers and text/location-only controls are absent, leaving the benefit of the multimodal language-model formulation insufficiently isolated.

Warning records are treated as event ground truth without independent verification of event occurrence. Absence of an issued warning does not necessarily establish normal weather, and the construction of negatives, simultaneous warning labels, and national reference answers is underspecified. These issues affect what the benchmark actually measures: reproducing issuance decisions versus detecting physical severe weather.

Aggregate accuracy gives an incomplete picture of severe-event performance. Gale accounts for approximately 42–44% of records, whereas the manuscript reports snowstorm accuracy at or below 6%. No macro-averaged performance, event precision/recall, or false-alarm analysis is provided. The T/F test balance is unspecified; given that roughly 88% of the complete dataset contains warnings, the reported 87.13% accuracy cannot be interpreted confidently without a majority baseline for that task. National generation also remains weak at 2.1/5.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent. The main text lists precipitation and pressure among the five variables, whereas the appendix specifies geopotential, u, v, temperature, and specific humidity. Normalization, spatial extent/resampling, Gaussian bandwidth, feature/token dimensions, and integration with each pretrained visual encoder are not adequately specified. Figure 2 includes a visual encoder, while the architectural prose describes projection into the LLM. These ambiguities materially limit reproducibility despite the useful training-parameter appendix.

The technical novelty is mainly an application-specific combination of temporal gating, Gaussian spatial weighting, and channel attention. Attention-weight plots do not substantiate the stronger claims of physical explanation or causal importance. Evaluation documentation also contains consequential inconsistencies: MC evaluation refers to four options despite the broader option set in the prompts, and the national scoring rubric substitutes fog for hail. Together with the forecasting mismatch and weak comparative controls, these concerns outweigh the promising dataset and ablation evidence in the submitted version.

strengths: MP-Bench is a potentially useful contribution to multimodal geospatial understanding: 421,363 records spanning seven severe-weather categories plus normal conditions, with four question formats. The 2023/2024 temporal split is preferable to randomly splitting highly correlated weather records.

Table 2 shows consistent improvements across four backbones. For Qwen2.5-VL, MC-main accuracy increases from 56.26% to 72.37% and macro-F1 from 26.88% to 50.88%, providing evidence that the proposed input-processing framework improves this benchmark.

The temporal, spatial, and channel modules provide sensible domain-specific inductive biases. The complete module-combination ablation in Table 3 supports the effectiveness of their joint use on the 5,000-sample subset.

The supplementary material supplies training configurations, task prompts, dataset distributions, and a judging rubric. Evaluation on 1,000 U.S. samples also provides preliminary evidence of geographic transfer.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not established by the experimental protocol. Section 3.1.2 supplies ERA5 reanalysis from [t, t+11] after warning issuance, incorporating future atmospheric information unavailable at issuance time. Although the introduction motivates interpreting operational NWP forecasts, no experiment uses forecasts available at t. The results therefore support retrospective warning reconstruction, not demonstrated early-warning capability; the temporal-window gains also reflect access to additional future information.

The labels are issued warnings rather than verified weather occurrences. Their issuance times do not necessarily identify event onset or duration, and a fixed 12-hour window does not resolve this distinction. The definition and verification of normal samples and the treatment of simultaneous weather types are insufficiently specified. This matters because MC requires one answer, while the supplementary error analysis explicitly identifies compound weather situations.

The main comparison confounds architecture with input information: baselines receive three surface-derived channels, while MMLM receives 185 variable–pressure-level channels. Table 3 partly addresses module effectiveness, but only on a small subset. There is no full-data comparison against a straightforward encoder using the same 185 channels, so the reported gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed fusion design. The individual gating, Gaussian masking, and attention mechanisms also offer limited methodological novelty.

Important evaluation checks are missing. Table 5 reports 88.05% severe-weather records in the 2024 set; if the T/F subset preserves this distribution, an always-Yes predictor would exceed the reported best 87.13% accuracy. Task-specific class proportions and balanced metrics are needed to resolve this concern. GPT-4o's 0.19% binary accuracy is also unexplained and warrants an audit of response parsing and abstentions before supporting conclusions about its meteorological understanding.

Evidence for detailed warning generation and transfer remains limited. The best MC-sub macro-F1 is 29.31%, and the best national-generation score is 2.1/5. National outputs are evaluated only by an unvalidated LLM judge, whose supplied rubric substitutes fog for hail. The U.S. evaluation reports no numerical baseline results or sufficient category-mapping details despite claiming superiority over baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete in consequential places: variable normalization, grid preprocessing, Gaussian width, fusion dimensions, and the connection to each backbone's visual encoder are not adequately specified. Normalization is especially important for DTGF's differences across variables with different units. The main text lists precipitation and pressure among the five variables, whereas Table 6 specifies geopotential, two wind components, temperature, and humidity. These gaps, together with the forecasting-protocol mismatch and evaluation concerns, outweigh the worthwhile dataset and empirical improvements and determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: MP-Bench is a potentially useful resource for meteorological multimodal learning: 421,363 records covering seven severe-weather categories plus normal conditions, 2,412 Chinese stations, and four question formats. The 2023/2024 train–test split is more convincing than a random split of closely related weather records.

Table 2 reports improvements across all four backbones. For Qwen2.5-VL, MC-main accuracy increases from 56.26% to 72.37% and macro-F1 from 26.88% to 50.88%, providing evidence that the richer inputs and proposed processing pipeline improve warning recognition.

The complete module-combination ablation in Table 3 supports the utility of combining temporal, spatial, and channel weighting on the smaller training subset. The mechanisms are understandable and relevant to processing meteorological grids.

The supplementary material supplies prompts, training configurations, dataset distributions, and a scoring rubric, and states that results average three runs. Testing on 1,000 U.S. samples also provides some evidence beyond the primary geographic domain.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim is not established by the evaluation. Section 3.1.2 supplies ERA5 reanalysis from [t, t+11], where t is warning issuance time. These future atmospheric fields are unavailable when issuing the warning. This is a valid retrospective interpretation task, but it does not demonstrate prospective prediction or warning generation from operational NWP outputs. No experiment measures performance using forecasts available at issuance time or quantifies the resulting distribution shift. This mismatch is the main reason the balance favors rejection.

The targets are issued warnings, not verified weather occurrences. Consequently, the reported metrics measure agreement with forecaster decisions rather than event forecasting accuracy. The construction does not adequately explain how normal cases are verified, how simultaneous warning types are handled in the single-answer MC task, or how station warnings become regional and national targets. The supplementary discussion explicitly identifies compound events as a source of apparent misclassification, making these labeling choices consequential.

The principal comparisons conflate input information with architectural improvements: Table 2 compares three surface-derived channels against 185 pressure-level channels plus the proposed modules. Table 3 partially addresses this through module ablations, but only with a 5,000-sample subset. A full-data, equal-input comparison with a conventional meteorological encoder is missing, as are text/location-only controls that would reveal reliance on geographic priors. The results support the combined pipeline more strongly than the claimed necessity or originality of its individual components.

There are substantive inconsistencies and omissions in the input specification. The main text describes temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure at 37 levels, whereas supplementary Table 6 lists geopotential, two wind components, temperature, and specific humidity. These are materially different inputs. Normalization, geographic grid dimensions, Gaussian width, fusion-layer configuration, and conversion into each backbone's visual representation are insufficiently specified. Normalization particularly matters because DTGF computes channelwise differences across variables with different units and scales.

Several evaluation results need stronger validation. GPT-4o's 0.19% accuracy on binary T/F questions is unexplained; parsing failures, refusals, or instruction mismatches should be separated from meteorological errors before concluding that the model lacks understanding. T/F class proportions are not reported, so 87.13% accuracy cannot be interpreted against a majority baseline; Table 5 shows that roughly 88% of the overall records are severe-weather cases, although the task-specific distribution may differ. Per-category recall and false-alarm rates would better establish usefulness for rare hazards.

Evidence for nationwide generation and geographic transfer remains limited. The best NSW score is 2.1/5, and the judge rubric lists Fog while omitting Hail, inconsistent with the benchmark taxonomy. There is no reported human agreement study or structured event-level precision/recall. The U.S. experiment reports 64.20% accuracy and 35.18% macro-F1 but omits numerical baseline results, detailed category mapping, and temporal alignment. These limitations do not negate the dataset's value, but they constrain the broader claims of reliable warning generation and generalization.

strengths: MP-Bench is a potentially useful contribution to multimodal pattern recognition: 421,363 records spanning seven severe-weather categories and normal conditions, 2,412 Chinese weather stations, and four QA formats. Preserving hourly fields and vertical atmospheric structure provides richer inputs than temporally averaged weather images.

The 2023 training/2024 testing split is a meaningful evaluation choice. The additional 1,000-sample U.S. evaluation provides preliminary evidence of geographic transfer, with 64.20% MC-main accuracy and 35.18% macro-F1.

Table 2 reports consistent improvements across four backbones. For Qwen2.5-VL, MC-main accuracy increases from 56.26% to 72.37%, and macro-F1 from 26.88% to 50.88%. These gains support the usefulness of the overall input-processing approach on the proposed benchmark.

The temporal gating, geographic masking, and text-conditioned channel weighting are understandable, domain-motivated components. Table 3 evaluates all eight module combinations and supports the effectiveness of their joint use on the 5,000-sample subset. The supplement supplies prompts, training settings, and additional analyses.
weaknesses: The principal concern is the mismatch between the forecasting claims and the evaluated information availability. Section 3.1.2 supplies ERA5 reanalysis from [t, t+11], where t is warning issuance. These future realized atmospheric fields would not be available when issuing that warning. The introduction proposes interpreting NWP forecasts, but no experiment substitutes forecasts available at issuance or measures sensitivity to forecast errors. The results support retrospective warning reconstruction from reanalysis; they do not establish prospective early-warning performance. This materially limits the central claim rather than merely requiring clearer terminology.

The main comparisons confound architecture with input information. Baselines receive three surface-variable channels, whereas MMLM receives 185 channels across five variables and 37 pressure levels. Consequently, Table 2 cannot attribute its gains specifically to the proposed fusion modules. The smaller matched-input ablation is useful, but does not establish the contribution at the full training scale. A competitive full-input encoder or supervised event classifier is also absent, leaving the advantage of the MLLM formulation over simpler structured prediction unresolved.

The dataset labels are issued warnings, not verified weather occurrences, yet several tasks describe detecting events that actually occur. The procedure for establishing normal conditions and resolving simultaneous warning types is insufficiently specified. This is consequential because MC requires one answer, while the supplement explicitly identifies compound rain-and-wind situations as apparent errors. The benchmark may penalize meteorologically valid additional events or learn warning-issuance practices without establishing actual hazard accuracy.

Evaluation reliability needs stronger support. GPT-4o's 0.19% binary accuracy is sufficiently anomalous that response validity and answer parsing should be audited before concluding that the model cannot understand meteorological inputs. T/F accuracy lacks task-specific class proportions and a majority baseline. NSW relies on an unvalidated LLM judge despite structured outputs that permit event-level precision and recall; its best score is only 2.1/5. Moreover, the supplied judging prompt substitutes Fog for Hail, contradicting the task vocabulary. Together, these issues weaken claims about discrimination and generated warning quality.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. The main text lists temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind speed, and pressure, while Table 6 specifies geopotential, u-wind, v-wind, temperature, and specific humidity. Table 2 also incorrectly describes channels as pressure levels. The manuscript does not adequately specify variable normalization, spatial preprocessing, Gaussian width, or the precise interface from fused 185-channel fields to each pretrained vision encoder. Normalization is especially consequential for DTGF's cross-channel Euclidean differences across heterogeneous physical units. These omissions limit reproducibility beyond ordinary presentation refinements.

The dataset and consistent benchmark gains are worthwhile, but the unsupported transition from future reanalysis to operational forecasting, compounded by comparison and evaluation ambiguities, currently outweigh the case for acceptance. The reported U.S. transfer and module ablations partly mitigate concerns, but do not resolve these central issues.
